title: California PERB Decision No. 3017E
summary: Description: Associated Chino Teachers (ACT) filed an unfair practice charge alleging that Chino Valley Unified School District violated the Educational Employment Relations Act when it (1) issued new regulations prohibiting most displays of flags in a manner that could reasonably be interpreted to prohibit EERA-protected activities, (2) unilaterally adopted those regulations without affording ACT adequate advance notice and an opportunity to bargain, (3) unilaterally adopted policies and regulations requiring employees to notify parents or guardians of student requests to change their gender identity, and (4) unilaterally replaced the parental notification policy with a revised policy and regulation. After a formal hearing, an Administrative Law Judge issued a proposed decision finding that the District’s flag display policy interfered with protected rights under EERA, and that the District violated EERA when it unilaterally adopted that policy. The proposed decision further found that the District violated EERA when it unilaterally adopted the student gender identity parental notification policy, and when it adopted some portions of the revised policy and regulation. The District filed exceptions challenging the interference finding as to the flag display policy, and the proposed decision’s reliance on the Board’s decision in Rocklin Unified School District (2025) PERB Decision No. 2939. Disposition: In a precedential decision, the Board found that the proposed decision did not err by finding that the District’s flag display policy interfered with employee rights to display union insignia and ACT’s right of reasonable access to District facilities to communicate with employees. The Board further found that the proposed decision did not err in relying on the Board’s precedential decision in Rocklin Unified School District (2025) PERB Decision No. 2939.
text:
STATE OF CALIFORNIA
DECISION OF THE
PUBLIC EMPLOYMENT RELATIONS BOARD
ASSOCIATED CHINO TEACHERS,
Charging Party,
Case No. LA-CE-6828-E
v.
PERB Decision No. 3017
CHINO VALLEY UNIFIED SCHOOL
April 20, 2026
DISTRICT,
Respondent.
Appearances: California Teachers Association by Stephanie J. Joseph and Megan
Degeneffe, Attorneys, for Associated Chino Teachers; Atkinson, Andelson, Loya,
Ruud & Romo by William A. Diedrich and David E. Robinett, Attorneys, for Chino
Valley Unified School District.
Before Krantz, Paulson, and Krausse, Members.
DECISION
PAULSON, Member: This case is before the Public Employment Relations
Board (PERB or Board) on exceptions by Chino Valley Unified School District to the
proposed decision of an administrative law judge (ALJ). The complaint alleged that the
District violated the Educational Employment Relations Act (EERA) by: (1) maintaining
a regulation that prohibits most displays of flags in a manner that can reasonably be
interpreted to prohibit EERA-protected activities; (2) unilaterally adopting that
regulation without affording Associated Chino Teachers (ACT) adequate advance
notice and opportunity to bargain; (3) unilaterally adopting and implementing a policy
requiring employees to notify parents or guardians of student requests to change their
gender identity; and (4) unilaterally replacing that policy with a revised policy and

regulation.1 The proposed decision found that the flag display policy could reasonably
be interpreted to infringe on EERA-protected rights, and that the District violated
EERA when it unilaterally adopted that policy. The proposed decision further found
that the District violated EERA when it unilaterally adopted the student gender identity
parental notification policy, and when it adopted portions of the revised policy and
regulation.
The exceptions in this matter implicate a narrower range of issues. The District
excepted to the proposed decision’s finding that the flag display policy tended to
interfere with EERA-protected rights, but not to the finding that it violated EERA when
it unilaterally adopted that policy. The District also excepted to the finding that it
violated EERA when it unilaterally adopted the student gender identity parental
notification policy, but no party excepted to any of the proposed decision’s findings
concerning the District’s unilateral adoption of the replacement policy. Those findings
not excepted to are not before us and remain binding on the parties. This includes the
proposed decision’s rescission remedy as to the flag display policy, which remedied
both the interference violation and the unilateral change allegations.
For the reasons we describe, we deny the District’s exceptions to the proposed
decision.
1 EERA is codified at Government Code section 3540 et seq. Further statutory
references are to the Government Code unless noted otherwise.
2

FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND2
I. The Parties
The District is a public school employer within the meaning of EERA section
3540.1(k). The District’s governing board is its five-member Board of Education
(BOE). Norm Enfield was the District’s Superintendent at all times relevant to this
dispute.
ACT is an “employee organization” and an “exclusive representative” within the
meaning of EERA sections 3540.1(d) and (e). ACT exclusively represents the
District’s certificated bargaining unit, which includes classroom teachers, behavioral
health and behavioral intervention counselors, nurses, psychologists, and librarians.
Some coaches for the District’s athletics programs are also certificated employees.
Brenda Walker was President of ACT until, on July 1, 2024, Steven Frazer was
elected as her successor.
ACT and the District were parties to a Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA)
effective from July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2025.
II. District Policies and Regulations
The District BOE adopts written policies and administrative regulations defining
the District’s mission and setting forth rules and standards for implementing that
mission.
BOE Bylaw 9310 governs the review, development, adoption, and revision of
policies. Proposed policies are presented for a first reading “for information” at a public
2 We recite only the facts relevant to the issues remaining in dispute.
3

BOE meeting. After this, the proposed policy may be submitted to a second reading at
a subsequent BOE meeting, where it is identified as an “action” item. However, each
member of the BOE has the right to raise an “action” item on a first reading and
thereby waive the second reading.
Bylaw 9310(a) includes language making any policy, bylaw, or administrative
regulation, or any portion thereof, inoperative “if it is found to be in conflict with
applicable federal or state law or regulations or court decisions.” This bylaw also
includes a severance and savings provision whereby the remainder of a policy will
remain in effect if any portion is found to be invalid.
Bylaw 9310(c) provides that either the Superintendent or the BOE may also
develop administrative regulations for the District’s operations. Administrative
regulations “may describe specific actions to be taken, roles and responsibilities of
staff, timelines, and/or other provisions,” and must be consistent with law and BOE
policies.
A. Display of Flags on District Property
BOE Policy (BP) 6115 governing Ceremonies and Observances provides:
“The Board of Education recognizes the importance of
having students observe holidays, celebrate events of
cultural or historical significance, and acknowledge the
contributions of outstanding individuals in society. On days
designated by the Board, staff shall provide students with
appropriate commemorative exercises so that they may
acquire the knowledge, skills, and principles essential for
informed, responsible citizenship in a democratic society.”
District Administrative Regulation (AR) 6115 implementing this policy prescribes
the time, location, and manner for displaying the flags of the United States and
4

California. It is undisputed that, prior to the events of this case, District employees
displayed various other flags on District property, including in classrooms during
instructional time.
1. The District Revises AR 6115
On or about June 9, 2023, the District posted on its website the agenda for its
June 15, 2023 BOE meeting. The agenda included an action item proposing revisions
to AR 6115 prohibiting the display of flags other than those of the United States and
California. The proposed revision added the following to AR 6115:
“No flag other than the United States of America and State
of California may be displayed unless it is a country, state,
or United States military flag used for educational purposes
within adopted curriculum. Any other flag must be approved
by the Superintendent or designee prior to displaying if and
only if it is used for purposes of education and only during
the related instructional period.
“Flags of higher education institutions shall be permitted as
part of the college and career program.”
The proposed revisions defined a flag as “a display of distinct color and design used
as a symbol, standard, signal, or emblem.” The agenda item also included a
memorandum from BOE President Sonja Shaw explaining that the revisions were
needed “to clearly define expectations related to patriotic exercises, and further
ensure that District-owned or leased property, including but not limited to classrooms,
[is] not being used as a platform for the display or promotion of political or social policy
matters, religious, or personal viewpoints, which are more often than not, deeply
rooted individual perspectives/opinions.”
5

There is no dispute that, apart from publicly posting the agenda on June 9,
2023, the District did not provide ACT notice of the proposed revisions to AR 6115. On
June 14, 2023, ACT President Walker sent a letter to members of the BOE asserting
that the proposed revisions infringed on employee rights under EERA, and that if the
BOE adopted the revisions without first giving ACT notice and an opportunity to
bargain over their impacts and effects on employees, the District would be violating its
duty to bargain in good faith. Superintendent Enfield, who was copied on Walker’s
letter, responded the same day. Enfield stated that the District was sensitive to ACT’s
concerns and offered to meet on dates after the June 15, 2023 BOE meeting.
On June 15, 2023, the District BOE approved the proposed revisions to
AR 6115 by a 4-to-1 vote.
2. The Parties’ Post-adoption Meetings Concerning AR 6115
On June 27, 2023, counsel for ACT, Stephanie Joseph, sent a letter to Enfield
reiterating and expanding on the points made by Walker in her June 14, 2023 letter.
Counsel asserted that employees could reasonably interpret the AR 6115 revisions as
prohibiting the display of union-related insignia and messages. Counsel also asserted
that because the revisions set out a prohibition on conduct in the workplace, violation
of which could lead to discipline, the District could not unilaterally implement the policy
without first meeting and conferring with ACT.
The parties met on June 28, 2023 for a little over one hour. ACT
representatives asked about discipline for violating the ban on displaying flags, and
counsel for the District, William Diedrich, responded that violations would be
addressed according to progressive discipline and the CBA. ACT also asked when the
6

District would begin enforcing the revised AR 6115. The District gave no firm date but
stated that it needed time to train administrators and staff before enforcement.
Diedrich also stated that the ban on flags did not implicate union speech or other
EERA-protected rights. The meeting ended without agreement on any issues.
On July 3, 2023, Diedrich sent the District’s response to ACT’s June 27, 2023
letter. According to Diedrich, the District believed that the revised AR 6115 did not
infringe on employees’ rights under EERA. Diedrich further asserted that the policy did
not prohibit union clothing or union buttons and allowed for flags with prior
administrative approval. With regard to ACT’s unilateral change allegations, Diedrich
asserted that notice had been given on June 14, 2023, and that enough time remained
for the parties to meet before the District completed training for administrators later in
July.
3. District Training on AR 6115
On August 4, 2023, one business day before the beginning of the District’s fall
semester, the District held an all-day mandatory training for staff regarding District
policy changes, including the revisions to AR 6115. Site administrators displayed
slides regarding AR 6115 prepared by a law firm representing the District. One slide
stated that AR 6115 did not apply to “[p]rotected union speech (i.e. EERA protected
communications, such as buttons),” protected student speech such as Tinker
armbands,3 or “colorful items that are not flags (such as floor mats, picture frames,
3 As the proposed decision notes, this was likely a reference to Tinker v. Des
Moines Independent Community School Dist. (1969) 393 U.S. 503, in which the United
States Supreme Court held that armbands worn by students in school to protest the
United States’ war against Vietnam were constitutionally protected speech, even if
7

etc.).” The same slide stated that the policy applied to duplications or facsimiles of
flags, such as a large photograph of a flag.
Steven Frazer, who was a biology teacher at Ruben S. Ayala High School at
the time, attended the training. In his testimony, Frazer recalled confusion and
uncertainty among educators over what constitutes a flag, what consequences would
ensue for violating the policy, and how the ban on certain materials would impact
student perceptions and expectations of the classroom as a safe place to explore
ideas. He testified that during the training, after teachers were presented with the text
of the revised AR 6115, District administrators instructed teachers to come up with
questions and find answers in small groups. Apart from the slides prepared by the
District’s attorneys, administrators did not answer teachers’ questions or address their
concerns.
Andrea McFarland is a high school English teacher who, at the time of her
testimony in this case, had worked 13 years as an English teacher including 10 years
with the District at Chino High School. She attended the training on August 4, 2023,
and also recalled confusion among teachers about what constituted a flag under
AR 6115. District administrators told staff that any flags or symbolism or
representation of any kind were now prohibited. McFarland’s impression was that “It
just sounded like everything needed to be taken down. And if it just symbolized
anything like, for example, a Dodgers flag or just anything [it] needed to be taken
school officials were concerned they might cause a disturbance on campus. (Id. at
pp. 505–514.)
8

down.”4 Teachers attending the August 4, 2023 training were required to sign a
document acknowledging that they had been made aware of their obligations under
AR 6115.
4. District Enforcement of AR 6115
Witnesses testified about a variety of flags, posters, photos, and other
depictions of flags that they were directed to remove pursuant to AR 6115 during the
2023-2024 school year. These included flags of countries other than the United
States, professional sports teams, and at least two items that included a rainbow
motif. One of the rainbow items was a poster displayed in a high school physics
classroom depicting the electromagnetic spectrum with the corresponding
wavelengths for the different colors.
Another was a “safe space card” that ACT provided to bargaining unit
employees. The card includes a header identifying its sponsor as the Lesbian Gay
Bisexual Transgender Queer+ Caucus of the California Teachers Association (CTA),
over a background image of color blocks arranged in typical rainbow order (red,
orange, yellow, green, blue, violet). On the other side of the card are the words “Safe
Space” and the same six colors arranged in horizontal bars. Beneath this, the card
states: “This is a safe and inclusive space for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender,
questioning, intersex, queer[+] students and their allies.”
4 While the District asserts that McFarland was only testifying about AR 6115’s
impact on flag displays in the classroom, as opposed to other areas on District
premises, this distinction is largely irrelevant, as we discuss in sections I and II below.
9

On November 7, 2023, ACT President Walker sent an e-mail to Associate
Superintendent of Human Resources Lea Fellows to “follow up” about a member
being instructed to remove the safe space card. Fellows confirmed on November 9,
2023 that “employee(s) have been asked to take down the card,” implying more than
one instance where this had happened. Walker asked on November 13, 2023 when
District administration had told site administrators that employees were not allowed to
display the safe space cards “in their rooms or work locations.” Fellows responded the
next day that the instruction had been given at the principals’ meeting on October 16,
2023. Superintendent Enfield also testified that a CTA safe space card with horizontal
lines in rainbow colors was a “flag” that would be prohibited by AR 6115.
B. Parental Notification Policies
No party excepted to the proposed decision’s finding that, before July 2023,
certificated employees were not required to notify parents or guardians of transgender
or gender non-conforming conduct, such as student requests to use gender
non-conforming nicknames, student disclosures to teachers that they were considering
a name or gender change, or other requests that do not implicate changing a student’s
permanent records. Furthermore, no party excepted to the proposed decision’s finding
that regardless of whether certificated employees were expected or required to inform
District administrators about student requests to change information in official or
unofficial records, before July 2023 they were not expected to notify parents or
guardians about such requests.
10

1. Adoption of BP 5020.1
At the same June 15, 2023 meeting during which the District adopted revisions
to AR 6115, the BOE considered for first public reading BP 5020.1, proposed to be a
new parental notification policy. BP 5020.1 required certificated employees to contact
a student’s parents or guardians in a variety of circumstances, only some of which are
at issue in this case.5
BP 5020.1, section 1 required certificated staff, including school counselors, to
notify parents or guardians, in writing, within three days if they become aware that a
student is requesting to be identified or treated as a gender other than that listed on
their birth certificate or in other official records. The policy specified that this would
include student requests to use a name that differs from their legal name, except
commonly recognized nicknames, or to use pronouns that do not align with the
student’s gender listed in official records. A student’s request to access
sex-segregated school programs or activities, including athletic teams and
competitions or bathrooms and changing facilities, that do not align with the student’s
gender listed on official records would also require parental notification.
More broadly, BP 5020.1, section 1 required parental notification for student
requests to change any information contained in their official or unofficial records.
BP 5020.1, section 4 required certificated staff to notify parents or guardians
within three days of “any incident or complaint of a verbal or physical altercation
5 ACT did not challenge BP 5020.1 sections 2 and 3, requiring parental
notification regarding student injuries and known or suspected suicidal intent or
behavior.
11

involving their child, including bullying by or against their child.” Unlike the provisions
for parental notification of gender nonconforming conduct, section 4 allowed
notification by telephone, mail, e-mail, or conference.
Because the BOE agendized BP 5020.1 “for information” at the June 15, 2023
meeting, no action was taken and no date for future action was specified.
On July 14, Walker discovered the agenda for the upcoming July 20, 2023 BOE
meeting on the District’s website. The agenda indicated that the BOE intended to vote
on BP 5020.1. There is no dispute that, apart from placing the item on the public
meeting agenda, the District did not provide notice to ACT that it proposed to create
new parental notification policies.
On July 20, 2023, the BOE adopted BP 5020.1 without amendment.
That same day, California Attorney General Rob Bonta sent a letter to Enfield
and BOE members advising them that BP 5020.1’s provisions requiring disclosure of
students’ transgender status, gender nonconforming conduct, and/or requests to
change information in their official or unofficial school records would, if enacted, likely
violate state and federal law, including constitutional rights of privacy and equal
protection. Bonta’s letter closed by indicating that the Attorney General’s Office “will
not hesitate to take action as appropriate to vigorously protect students’ civil rights.”
On July 28, 2023, Walker sent an e-mail to Enfield asserting that in light of
Bonta’s letter, BP 5020.1 was unlawful and demanding that the District withdraw it and
cease implementation. In the alternative, Walker’s e-mail to Enfield asserted that BP
5020.1 affected several negotiable matters and demanded that if not withdrawn, the
District must meet and negotiate with ACT regarding its impacts and effects on
12

employee evaluations, discipline, and other subjects ostensibly covered by the CBA,
including Article 3.11 (Consultation), Article 4 (District Rights), Article 9 (Personnel File
Contents and Inspection), Article 10 (Public Charges), Article 12.18 (Working
Conditions), and Article 20 (Miscellaneous).
At some point thereafter not reflected in the record, the Attorney General filed
suit on behalf of the State of California against the District in San Bernardino Superior
Court. On September 6, 2023, the superior court granted the State’s request for a
temporary restraining order (TRO) regarding BP 5020.1. The TRO restrained and
enjoined the District from “adopting, implementing, enforcing, or otherwise giving
effect” to certain portions of BP 5020.1.
Also on September 6, 2023, Enfield sent a message informing District
employees of the superior court’s decision to grant the requested TRO and place a
“short-term hold” on some but not all of BP 5020.1’s parental notification provisions.
Enfield’s message did not identify the sections of BP 5020.1 that had been enjoined.
Instead, it advised employees that while awaiting the court’s final order, “we anticipate
[that] only the parental notifications related to name and pronoun changes, and access
to sex-segregated facilities, programs and athletics will be put in abeyance.” Enfield’s
message speculated that all other provisions of the policy were “likely to remain in
place.”
On October 19, 2023, the superior court issued a preliminary injunction against
BP 5020.1 sections 1(a) and 1(b). The court’s order left in place BP 5020.1’s
13

provisions requiring parental notification for student requests to change information in
official or unofficial records and for all physical or verbal student altercations.6
On February 27, 2024, the District’s Human Resources Department provided
ACT with a “Consult Notification” form indicating that the District was considering
adopting BP and AR 5010, a new board policy and associated regulation regarding
parental notification. The form referenced CBA sections 3.11.1 and 3.12.1 and stated
that consultation includes an opportunity for input, proposals, and recommendations
before the District acts.
BP 5010 repeats verbatim provisions of BP 5020.1 requiring parental
notification for student requests to change information contained in their official or
unofficial records, and of any “verbal or physical altercation” involving a student.
However, unlike BP 5020.1, BP 5010 omits any reference to gender identity or gender
expression as triggering a parental notification requirement. BP 5010 also includes a
new requirement for parental notification of a student’s participation in
“school-sponsored extracurricular and cocurricular activities or team(s).”
Implementing this policy, AR 5010 creates a two-step process where
certificated staff must notify a designated District administrator “immediately” of a
student’s request to change official or unofficial records; that administrator is then
responsible for further steps in the parental notification process. On the other hand,
AR 5010 maintained AR 5020.1’s one-step direct parental notification process for
student altercations.
6 On October 3, 2024, the superior court issued a final judgment and permanent
injunction against BP 5020.1 sections 1(a) and 1(b). The District did not appeal.
14

On March 3, 2024, ACT sent a letter to Enfield which asserted that the
proposed BP and AR 5010 affected unit members’ job duties, discipline, evaluations
and other conditions of employment; demanded to bargain “the policies and/or their
impacts and effects”; asked for information about the proposed policy and regulation;
and requested that the District refrain from implementation until the parties had
completed negotiations over the proposed changes and their effects. Among the
information ACT requested was the District’s position regarding whether BP and AR
5010 were intended to replace BP 5020.1, whether BP 5020.1 would be rescinded,
and proposed dates of implementation. ACT’s information request asked the District to
provide responses by the close of business on March 6, 2024. However, the District
did not respond before it took up the proposed policy and regulation at its next BOE
meeting.
On March 7, 2024, BOE voted 4-1 to adopt BP and AR 5010. As a separate
“consent” item on its agenda, BOE decided to “delete” BP 5020.1.
III. The Proposed Decision
The proposed decision found violations as to ACT’s unilateral change
allegations and interference allegations pertaining to AR 6115. Relying primarily on
our decision in Rocklin Unified School District (2025) PERB Decision No. 2939
(Rocklin), the proposed decision also sustained the unilateral change allegation
regarding the District’s adoption of BP 5020.1. The proposed decision partially
sustained the unilateral change allegations with respect to the District’s passage of BP
5010, finding only some challenged portions of that policy were negotiable. To remedy
these violations, the proposed decision ordered the District to cease and desist the
15

unlawful conduct, make employees whole for any losses caused by the violations, and
post a notice. Because rescission of unlawfully adopted policies is generally the
appropriate remedy to restore the status quo and ensure a level playing field for future
negotiations, the proposed decision ordered the District to rescind the revisions to AR
6115 as well as the offending provisions of BP 5010. However, because the BP
5020.1 was no longer in effect, no rescission was needed to fully remedy the District’s
unlawful adoption of that policy.
No party filed exceptions to the proposed decision’s treatment of BP 5010, and
so those issues are not before us. Although the District filed exceptions to the
proposed decision’s findings related to the AR 6115 interference allegation, it did not
contest the unilateral change violation concerning that policy, nor did it object to the
proposed rescission remedy.
The District’s exceptions concerning BP 5020.1 do not challenge any of the
specific findings in the proposed decision supporting the elements of the violation.
Instead, the District asserts simply that the proposed decision erred by relying on
Rocklin, supra, PERB Decision No. 2939, because that decision was not final and still
subject to judicial review.
DISCUSSION
When resolving exceptions to a proposed decision, the Board applies a de novo
standard of review. (County of Santa Clara (2019) PERB Decision No. 2629-M, p. 6.)
However, to the extent that a proposed decision has adequately addressed issues
raised by certain exceptions, the Board need not further analyze those exceptions.
16

(Ibid.) The Board also need not address alleged errors that would not affect the
outcome. (City of San Ramon (2018) PERB Decision No. 2571-M, p. 5.)
I. EERA Grants Public School Employees the Right to Display Union Insignia
To establish a prima facie interference case, a charging party must show that
an employer’s conduct tends to or does result in some harm to protected union and/or
employee rights. (City of San Diego (2020) PERB Decision No. 2747-M, p. 36 (San
Diego).) A charging party need not establish that the employer acted because of an
unlawful motive. (Claremont Unified School District (2019) PERB Decision No. 2654,
p. 20.)
If a charging party establishes a prima facie case, the burden shifts to the
employer. (San Diego, supra, PERB Decision No. 2747-M, p. 36.) The degree of harm
dictates the employer’s burden. (Ibid.) If the harm is “inherently destructive” of
protected rights, the employer must show that the interference results from
circumstances beyond its control and that no alternative course of action was
available. (Ibid.) For conduct that is not inherently destructive, the respondent may
attempt to justify its actions based on operational necessity. (Ibid.) In such cases,
PERB balances the asserted business need against the tendency to harm protected
rights; if the tendency to harm outweighs the necessity, PERB finds a
violation. (Ibid.) Within the category of actions or rules that are not inherently
destructive, the stronger the tendency to harm, the greater is the respondent’s burden
to show its business need was important and that it narrowly tailored its actions or
rules to attain that purpose while limiting harm to protected rights as much as
possible. (Id. at pp. 36-37, fn. 19.) In cases involving employer speech, the accuracy
17

of the communication is relevant to whether the employer can establish an affirmative
defense. (Id. at p. 37.)
California’s public sector employees, like private sector employees, have a right
to display union insignia in the workplace, absent an employer’s proof of “special
circumstances” justifying a prohibition. (State of California (Department of Parks and
Recreation) (1993) PERB Decision No. 1026-S, p. 5.) PERB has applied this rule in a
wide range of employment contexts. (See, e.g., East Whittier School District (2004)
PERB Decision No. 1727 [classroom teachers] (East Whittier); County of Sacramento
(2014) PERB Decision No. 2393-M [firefighters]; Fresno County Superior Court (2017)
PERB Decision No. 2517-C, vacated in part on other grounds by Fresno County
Superior Court (2019) PERB Decision No. 2517a-C [trial court employees]; Regents of
the University of California (2018) PERB Decision No. 2616-H [hospital workers in
patient care areas] (Regents); Regents of the University of California (2023) PERB
Decision No. 2880-H [skilled trades employees affixing magnets to work trucks].)
Precedent distinguishes employees’ right to engage in solicitation and
distribution of literature from the “far less disruptive” protected display of union
insignia. In the case of solicitation and distribution of literature, “restrictions on
employee solicitation, including the distribution of union literature, during non-work
time and in non-work areas are invalid, unless the employer shows that special
circumstances make such rules necessary to maintain production or discipline.”
(Petaluma City Elementary School District/Joint Union High School District (2016)
PERB Decision No. 2485, p. 46, emphasis added.) Thus, employer rules prohibiting
18

such conduct on the employer’s property are presumptively unlawful, because they
apply when employees are off-duty or are in non-working areas. (Id. at p. 45.)
However, employees’ presumptive right to display union insignia is not limited
to non-working time or to non-work areas. (Regents, supra, PERB Decision
No. 2616-H, pp. 13-14.) Unlike solicitation and distribution of literature, a display of
union insignia does not inherently involve an interruption from work. (Ibid.) PERB has
specifically held that “as a general rule the right to wear union buttons attaches in
instructional settings as it does elsewhere.” (East Whittier, supra, PERB Decision
No. 1727, p. 11.)
The employer’s burden to prove special circumstances is resolved on a
case-by-case basis, and requires a concrete, fact-based evidentiary showing justifying
a narrowly tailored restriction. (State of California (Department of Corrections and
Rehabilitation) (2024) PERB Decision No. 2926-S, p. 21.) Typically, relevant factors
include whether an insignia or message is likely to negatively affect operations, such
as by posing a safety risk, disrupting employee discipline, distracting from work
demanding great concentration, or damaging employer property. (Ibid.) The specific
context of the restriction is also relevant, including industry practices and the parties’
past practice. (Ibid.) “Thus, a history of insignia or messages in the workplace without
resulting incidents can undercut an employer’s argument.” (Ibid.)
The Board has also recognized that a school district has an interest in
educating its students in classrooms free from undue distraction and disruption. (East
Whittier, supra, PERB Decision No. 1727, p. 11.) However, the mere possibility of
disruption is not sufficient to establish a special circumstance justifying a prohibition
19

on displaying union insignia in a classroom. Instead, we compare the distraction
caused by the display of union insignia “with other distractions permitted or fostered by
[a school district] to enhance the sense of community among the students.” (Id. at
pp. 11-12.) As part of this inquiry, we must consider the actual nature of the insignia at
issue. (Id. at p. 12.) Because some union insignia are more controversial than others,
the fact-intensive special circumstances test disfavors one-size-fits-all rules. (Id. at
pp. 11-12; see also Regents, supra, PERB Decision No. 2616-H, pp. 14-15.)
II. AR 6115 Tends to Restrict Employees’ Protected Right to Display Union
Insignia
The District’s exceptions are largely devoted to establishing that the proposed
decision erred by finding that AR 6115 applied during non-work time or in non-work
areas, such as break rooms, teachers’ lounges, or parking lots. For the reasons we
have just explained, this issue is largely a red herring. Unlike solicitation and
distribution of literature, there is no presumption of validity for rules restricting the
display of union insignia in the classroom. (East Whittier, supra, PERB Decision
No. 1727, p. 11.) The employer must make a concrete, fact-based showing of special
circumstances justifying a narrowly tailored restriction on any display of union insignia.
(Ibid.) Although the employer’s interest in minimizing disruptions to instruction can
potentially form the basis for such a showing, the outcome depends on the actual
evidence of a display’s tendency to distract from education, compared to other
permitted displays in the classroom. (Id. at pp. 11-12.)
Even so, the proposed decision did not err by concluding that AR 6115 also
applies during non-work time and in non-work areas. Attempting to show otherwise,
the District downplays the significance of BOE President Shaw’s memorandum,
20

written on District letterhead and sent in her capacity as BOE President to her fellow
BOE members in advance of their vote. Although acknowledging that Shaw’s
memorandum stated that the policy would apply “on District property,” and thus not
merely in classrooms, the District contends that Shaw was not speaking on behalf of
the District as a whole.
We reject the District’s argument because it ignores basic statutory
interpretation principles. To determine intent, courts first look to the words of the
statute because they are the most reliable indicator of legislative intent. (People
v. Lopez (2003) 31 Cal.4th 1051, 1056.) If the statutory language is clear and
unambiguous, the plain meaning of the statute governs. (Ibid.) Here, AR 6115
contains no language limiting its scope to classrooms alone. Indeed, its provisions for
the display of the flags of the United States and California apply expressly to
non-classroom locations on District property.
To the extent that AR 6115’s text leaves any ambiguity that it was intended to
apply to District property generally, the proposed decision did not err by relying on
Shaw’s memorandum for further evidence. If a statute’s text is susceptible to more
than one reasonable construction, courts look to “a variety of extrinsic aids.” (People
v. Lopez, supra, 31 Cal.4th 1051, 1056.) This includes the explanatory materials, like
committee reports, that are presented to legislators when voting on a bill. As the
California Supreme Court has explained, “it is reasonable to infer that those who
actually voted on the proposed measure read and considered the materials presented
in explanation of it, and that the materials therefore provide some indication of how the
measure was understood at the time by those who voted to enact it.” (Hutnick v. U.S.
21

Fidelity & Guaranty Co. (1988) 47 Cal.3d 456, 465, fn. 7.) While Shaw’s memorandum
is not strictly a “committee report,” it serves a similar function and is the only
explanatory material provided in the June 15, 2023 agenda that would aid BOE
members in understanding the meaning of the revisions to AR 6115. Shaw’s
memorandum is clear that the revised policy applied on “District-owned or leased
property, including but not limited to classrooms.”
Furthermore, the proposed decision did not err when it found that the revised
AR 6115’s ban on all flags, depictions of flags, symbols, or insignia included union
insignia. Again, we look first to AR 6115’s text to determine its intended function. Here,
there is no doubt that union insignia are included within the policy’s extremely broad
definition of flags: “A flag is defined as a display of distinct color and design used as a
symbol, standard, signal, or emblem.” Plainly, this language encompasses union
insignia.
The District’s exceptions urge us to disregard AR 6115’s broad text in favor of
the training materials its attorneys prepared after the revisions went into effect. Those
materials asserted that the restriction on flags did not apply to “[p]rotected union
speech (i.e. EERA protected communications, such as buttons).” Because the text of
AR 6115 is clear, by virtue of its extremely broad definitions, there is no cause to
resort to extrinsic evidence of its meaning. (People v. Lopez, supra, 31 Cal.4th 1051,
1056.) Further, the District’s training materials were developed post-enactment, and
therefore would not constitute controlling evidence of the BOE’s intent in voting to
approve the revisions to AR 6115. (See Metropolitan Water Dist. of Southern
California v. Imperial Irr. Dist. (2000) 80 Cal.App.4th 1403, 1437, fn. 17
22

[post-enrollment materials are not legislative history to be considered by reviewing
courts].) But even so, the District enforced AR 6115 against union insignia when it
required teachers to remove “safe space” placards that contained union logos.
“In the area of employer rules and directives, PERB does not look favorably on
broad, vague directives that might chill lawful speech or other protected conduct.” (Los
Angeles Community College District (2014) PERB Decision No. 2404, p. 6.) We
cannot say that AR 6115 is “vague,” but only because it is so startlingly broad that it
could reasonably encompass any symbolic representation of anything. Irrespective of
enforcement, a rule that bans a category of conduct that could include protected
activity as well as unprotected activity is unlawful because of this tendency to chill
protected activity. (Santee Elementary School District (2006) PERB Decision
No. 1822, pp. 11-13.) This is the case with the revisions to AR 6115.
The proposed decision found that there was no evidence that the revisions to
AR 6115 were intended to ensure safe operations, maintain discipline, protect District
property, or prevent disruptive, obscene, violent, or otherwise unprotected speech or
unauthorized concerted activity. Nor was there any evidence that the new policy was
responsive to any parent, student, employee, or management complaint. The District
did not except to these conclusions, only that it was required to show them for the
reasons we have already discussed and rejected. Absent a concrete, fact-based
evidentiary showing, we cannot find that special circumstances justify AR 6115’s
restriction on the display of union insignia, whether on District property inside or
outside of the classroom.
23

For these reasons, the District violated EERA section 3543.5(a) by adopting
and maintaining revisions to AR 6115 that ban employee displays of union insignia.
III. AR 6115 Unreasonably Restricts Union Access Rights
AR 6115’s broad restriction on insignia, including union insignia, also interferes
with ACT’s organizational rights. As we have repeatedly noted, “harm to employees’
protected rights and the harm to employee organizations’ protected rights are
inseparable in this factual setting.” (County of Sacramento, supra, PERB Decision
No. 2393-M, p. 33; accord State of California (Department of Corrections and
Rehabilitation), supra, PERB Decision No. 2926-S, pp. 20-23.)
A union’s right to display insignia in the workplace is rooted, in part, in its right
to communicate with the employees it represents. (County of Sacramento, supra,
PERB Decision No. 2393-M, p. 33.) An employer must allow an exclusive
representative reasonable access to employer property and other means of
communication with bargaining unit employees. (EERA, § 3543.1(b); see generally
County of San Joaquin (2021) PERB Decision No. 2775-M, pp. 26-39.) An employer
bears the burden of proving that a restriction on such rights is: (1) necessary for safe
or efficient operations; and (2) narrowly drawn to avoid overbroad, unnecessary
interference with protected rights. (Id. at pp. 26-27.)
As the proposed decision explained, to the extent ACT wishes to communicate
with employees with posters, fliers, newsletters, or other graphic or printed materials
containing a “flag,” depiction of a flag, or other recognizable symbol or insignia,
AR 6115 prohibits it from doing so on bulletin boards, in mailboxes, and by any other
means of communication, contrary to EERA section 3543.1(b). For the same reasons
24

we affirm the proposed decision’s reasoning that AR 6115 restricts the display of
union insignia, including in non-working areas and during non-working time, we affirm
that its maintenance also violates ACT’s right of reasonable access to District facilities
and to represent employees, thereby violating EERA sections 3543.1(b) and
3543.5(b).
IV. Rocklin is Binding Authority Unless and Until it is Overturned and the Proposed
Decision was Correct to Rely on it.
As noted above, the proposed decision relied heavily on the Board’s decision in
Rocklin, supra, PERB Decision No. 2939 in its discussion of the negotiability of
BP 5020.1. In Rocklin we found a parental notification policy that was “substantially
similar” to BP 5020.1 was within the scope of negotiation under EERA because it
required a change in teachers’ job duties, workload, qualifications, or performance
standards. (Id. at p. 28.) There, teachers were previously permitted to disclose a
student’s transgender or gender nonconforming identity without the student’s consent
only when required by law or to preserve the student’s physical or mental well-being.
(Ibid.) The Rocklin school district’s new policy created new duties that were not
“reasonably comprehended” within the teachers’ prior assignments, and were thus
negotiable. (Id. at p. 30.)7
Even when an employer has no obligation to bargain over a particular decision,
it nonetheless must provide notice and an opportunity to bargain in good faith over any
7 We also found that the Rocklin parental notification policy was negotiable
under the Board’s longstanding test for unenumerated subjects of bargaining
established by Anaheim Union High School District (1981) PERB Decision No. 177
(the “Anaheim framework”). (Rocklin, supra, PERB Decision No. 2939, p. 31.)
25

reasonably foreseeable effects the decision may have on matters within the scope of
representation. (County of Santa Clara (2019) PERB Decision No. 2680-M, pp. 11-12.)
However, matters prohibited by external law or public policy may not be negotiated or
included in a collective bargaining agreement, even if the parties were to agree to do
so. (City of San Jose (2013) PERB Decision No. 2341-M, p. 44.) The school district in
Rocklin sought to negotiate with its teachers’ union over the implementation of its
policy, but the union refused unless the district first rescinded the policy. (Rocklin,
supra, PERB Decision No. 2939, p. 35.) We found that because the parental
notification policy “violate[d] the California Constitution and multiple state laws,
including the SAFETY Act,8 by singling out transgender and gender nonconforming
students for different, adverse treatment that puts them at risk of harm,” any proposals
the school district could make regarding implementation would be illegal. (Id. at pp. 35,
36.) Thus, under the unusual circumstances of the case, even though the school
district was willing to negotiate over implementation, it would have been impossible to
bargain in good faith. (Ibid.)
The District’s exceptions challenge the proposed decision’s reliance on these
holdings because Rocklin was pending judicial review before the California Court of
Appeal, Third Appellate District at the time. However, since then, on October 31, 2025,
the Court of Appeal summarily denied the school district’s petition for writ of
extraordinary relief. Then, on January 14, 2026, the California Supreme Court denied
the school district’s petition for review.
8 Statutes 2024, chapter 95.
26

In fact, “all decisions and orders issued by the Board itself are precedential and
may be cited in any matter pending before a Board agent or the Board itself,” unless
they are expressly designated otherwise. (PERB Reg. 32320(c) [emphasis added].)9
That a recent decision is subject to judicial review is of no consequence to this rule.
PERB’s practice of identifying decisions that have been appealed on its website is a
service to its constituents and legal researchers and does not constitute a
determination that the decision is non-precedential under PERB Regulation 32320.
The only authority the District cites in support of its claim that decisions pending
judicial review may not be cited as precedent are two proposed decisions by
administrative law judges. These proposed decisions, which were never adopted by
the Board itself, are not precedential, unlike Rocklin. (PERB Reg. 32215.)
The District also points to unsettled litigation surrounding parental notifications
more generally. These issues are not before us. We note, however, that even if
parental notification policies like the District’s are eventually found lawful, that would
not affect the outcome of this case. Here, the proposed decision found that BP 5020.1
imposed new duties on certificated employees that were not reasonably
comprehended within existing job duties. Thus, the District was not privileged to adopt
those policies without first bargaining with ACT in good faith to agreement or an
overall impasse in negotiations and all applicable impasse resolution procedures.
(Bellflower Unified School District (2021) PERB Decision No. 2796, p. 9.) The District
filed no exceptions to these findings; in any event, for the same reasons the ALJ
9 PERB Regulations are codified at Cal. Code Regs., tit. 8, § 31001 et seq.
27

explained, we would find that the District failed to bargain in good faith even if
BP 5020.1 had been otherwise lawful. Further, because the District unilaterally
replaced BP 5020.1 with a new policy that is no longer in dispute, no party seeks
negotiations over its implementation.
For these reasons, we deny the District’s exceptions objecting to the proposed
decision’s reliance on Rocklin, supra, PERB Decision No. 2939. The proposed
decision correctly applied the Board’s precedent.
V. Remedy
PERB has broad powers to remedy unfair practices, including the power to
direct an offending party to cease and desist its unlawful conduct and to take such
affirmative action, including but not limited to reinstatement of employees with or
without back pay, as the Board deems necessary to effectuate the policies and
purposes of EERA. (Gov. Code, §§ 3541.3, 3541.5(c); Bellflower Unified School
District (2022) PERB Decision No. 2544a, pp. 25-26, 44; City of Pasadena (2014)
PERB Order No. Ad-406-M, p. 12.) In addition to a cease-and-desist order and notice
posting, an appropriate remedy for employer interference with protected rights may
include restoration of the prior status quo, including reinstatement of employees with
or without back pay, as PERB deems necessary to effectuate the policies of EERA.
(EERA, § 3541.5(c); Santa Monica Community College District v. Public Employment
Relations Bd. (1980) 112 Cal.App.3d 684, 691–692; Contra Costa County Fire
Protection District (2019) PERB Decision No. 2632-M, pp. 57-58.) A return to the prior
status quo and make-whole relief are also necessary to remedy unlawful unilateral
changes and ensure that future negotiations proceed on a level playing field. (City of
28

San Diego (2015) PERB Decision No. 2464-M, p. 40; County of Santa Clara (2013)
PERB Decision No. 2321-M, p. 24.)
As we have already noted, much of the ALJ’s proposed remedy is not before
us. Perhaps most significantly, the ALJ’s proposed order directed the District to
rescind AR 6115 based on both the conclusion that it interfered with employee and
employee organization rights, and that its unilateral enactment violated the District’s
duty to bargain in good faith to impasse or agreement with ACT. Although the District
did not except to the unilateral change finding, our discussion in section II above
further illustrates why the matter was appropriate for bargaining. Under the “Anaheim
framework,” a non-enumerated issue falls within the scope of representation if: (1) it is
logically and reasonably related to wages, hours, or an enumerated term and
condition of employment (i.e., it involves the employment relationship); (2) the subject
is of such concern to management and employees that conflict is likely to occur, and
the mediatory influence of collective negotiations is the appropriate means of resolving
the conflict; and (3) the employer’s obligation to negotiate would not significantly
abridge its freedom to exercise those managerial prerogatives (including matters of
fundamental policy) essential to the achievement of the employer’s mission. (San
Mateo City School Dist. v. Public Employment Relations Bd. (1983) 33 Cal.3d 850,
857-858.) In certain applications, AR 6115 amounts to a dress code, which is a
mandatory subject of bargaining. (Trustees of the California State University (2001)
PERB Decision No. 1451-H, adopting proposed decision at pp. 7-8.) AR 6115 is also
negotiable because it affects ACT’s ability to communicate with bargaining unit
members during non-working time and in non-work areas. (Regents of the University
29

of California (2012) PERB Decision No. 2300-H, pp. 20-27.) Furthermore, the
uncontested evidence showed widespread confusion over AR 6115’s breadth, and
that employees could face discipline for violations. If the District’s position is that it
never intended to penalize protected activity, negotiations could have proven it.
Having denied the District’s exceptions, we affirm the ALJ’s proposed remedial
order.
ORDER
Upon the foregoing findings of fact and conclusions of law, and the entire
record in the case, the Public Employment Relations Board finds that Chino Valley
Unified School District (District) violated the Educational Employment Relations Act
(EERA), Government Code sections 3543.5(a) and (b) by adopting and maintaining
revisions to Administrative Regulation (AR) 6115, “Ceremonies and Observances,”
which interfere with employee and employee organization rights. The District also
violated its duty to meet and negotiate in good faith and derivatively interfered with
protected rights, in violation of EERA sections 3543.5(c), (a) and (b), by: (1) adopting
the above-referenced revisions to AR 6115 without providing reasonable notice and
meaningful opportunity for bargaining to Associated Chino Teachers, CTA/NEA (ACT),
which is the exclusive representative of the District’s certificated employees;
(2) adopting Board Policy (BP) 5020.1 containing parental notification provisions
without providing reasonable notice and meaningful opportunity for bargaining to ACT;
and (3) adopting BP 5010(c) section 5 and AR 5010(e), without providing reasonable
notice and meaningful opportunity for bargaining to ACT.
30

Pursuant to sections 3541.3 and 3541.5 of EERA, it is hereby ORDERED that
the District, its governing board and its representatives shall:
A. CEASE AND DESIST FROM:
1. Adopting, revising, and/or maintaining governing board policies
and/or administrative regulations that employees and ACT could reasonably interpret
as prohibiting protected activities under EERA.
2. Adopting or revising governing board policies and/or
administrative regulations affecting certificated employees’ terms and conditions of
employment without providing ACT with reasonable notice and meaningful opportunity
for bargaining.
3. Interfering with employees’ right to be represented by ACT.
4. Denying ACT the right to represent its bargaining unit employees.

THE POLICIES OF EERA:
1. Rescind all revisions to AR 6115 adopted by the District on

2. Upon ACT’s request, meet and negotiate in good faith with ACT
